e.t: This LXX proper name identifies a person called “Adōnibezek,” also rendered “Athonivezek.” It functions as a personal name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament, in Joshua and Judges. Without the surrounding verse text, its significance here is limited to identifying the individual who bears this name.

This word describes a “breach of faith” or “transgression”—a failure to remain faithful or a violation of what is required. As a noun, it names the offense itself; it can also function adjectivally to describe something characterized by such unfaithfulness. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in 1 Kings, 2 Chronicles, and Jeremiah. Its central idea is a departure from faithfulness, expressed as wrongdoing or disobedience. The precise force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding verse.

This noun refers to a “section” or “sect”—a distinct division or group. It can identify people understood as a separate faction rather than as the whole community. In the Greek Old Testament and related writings represented here, it occurs four times: three times in the Old Testament and once in 1 Maccabees. Its exact force in any passage depends on the surrounding wording, but the central idea is a separated section or group. The word is found in Genesis 49:5, Leviticus 22:18 and 22:21, and 1 Maccabees 8:30.

This word means “shamefully,” describing an action done in a dishonorable, disgraceful, or improper manner. As an adverb, it tells how someone acts rather than naming a person, object, or action itself. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs twice, showing a manner of conduct marked by shame or dishonor. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This adjective describes someone or something as ingenuous—open and without deceit—or uncontaminated, free from what would spoil its purity. It presents a quality of clean-hearted simplicity rather than clever manipulation or mixture with corruption. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Esther 8:12. Because the surrounding verse text is not provided here, its exact emphasis in that occurrence cannot be specified; its ordinary meaning remains a description of what is sincere, untainted, or free from contamination.

It means “from another place,” describing where someone or something comes from or is located in relation to a different place. As an adverb, it modifies an action or statement by pointing away from the place already in view toward another location. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Esther 4:14. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain its particular force there, but its basic sense remains a reference to a different place.

This verb means “mow”: to cut down grass or standing crops as part of harvesting. In the Greek Old Testament, it describes the action of cutting vegetation in agricultural settings. It occurs five times, in five verses, appearing in Leviticus, Deuteronomy, Isaiah, and Micah. Its precise force in any one verse depends on whether the surrounding passage speaks of cultivated crops, grass, or the results of a harvest.

Amman is a proper name, used as a specific designation rather than as a general descriptive word. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times across five verses, from Genesis through 2 Samuel. Its meaning is simply the name “Amman”; the available lexical information does not establish an additional ordinary sense or explain whether each occurrence refers to a person, place, or people-group. The surrounding verse determines that specific reference.

This verb means to bend back or revert—to turn back toward an earlier direction or state. It describes a change of course, whether something physically turns back or a person or situation returns. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 12 times, showing a recurring action rather than a rare technical term. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on what is turning back and the surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX verb means “pick up” or “gather up.” It describes collecting something and bringing it together, rather than leaving it scattered. The word appears three times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical corpus, including passages in 1 Samuel, 1 Kings, and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one verse depends on what is being collected and the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains taking up or gathering together.

This verb means “die in requital”—to die as a response to what has been done. It expresses dying in return, rather than simply describing death in general. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, in Exodus 22:2. The exact force of the word in that verse belongs with the surrounding passage, but its lexical idea is death understood as requital or return.

This word means a representation or likeness—something that resembles or portrays another thing. As a noun, it refers to an image or visible depiction rather than the thing represented itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Wisdom 13:10. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument, but the word’s basic idea remains a likeness or representation. It can therefore describe something fashioned to resemble another reality, especially when distinguishing an image from what it is intended to portray.

This verb means to scatter people or things abroad, causing them to spread apart rather than remain together. It expresses the act of dispersing or sending something in different directions. In the Greek text of 4 Maccabees, it occurs once, at 4 Maccabees 5:11; the surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what is being dispersed there. Its central idea remains clear: separation into separate places or groups.

This proper noun refers to people called “Araps.” It functions as a people-group name rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented by this LXX corpus, it occurs 14 times, including passages in 2 Chronicles, Nehemiah, Psalms, Isaiah, and the Maccabean books. Its basic meaning identifies the named people; the surrounding verse is needed to determine what they are doing or how they relate to the passage.

e.h: A Personal Name: Hares or Ares
e.t: This word is a proper name, referring to a person named Hares, also rendered Ares. It is not a common noun describing an action, quality, or object, but identifies an individual. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, in Judges 8:13. The precise role of the named person in that verse belongs to the surrounding passage, but the word itself functions as a personal designation rather than a general description.

Arisoth is a proper name, used to identify a particular named entity rather than to describe an action, quality, or general idea. It is rendered consistently as “Arisoth,” so the available lexical information gives the name itself without a separate descriptive meaning. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Judges 4:2, 4:13, and 4:16. Its precise referent in each verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Asabias, also rendered Asavias, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times, each time identifying a person in passages from 1 Chronicles and Nehemiah. Because the name is used for individuals, its basic meaning is its function as a personal designation. The surrounding verse is needed to identify which Asabias is meant and what that person does in each passage.

Asordan is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or ordinary object. It is also represented as “Asorthan,” showing a related form of the same name. This name occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus, once in 2 Kings 19:37 and once in Isaiah 37:38. The available information identifies the name and its occurrences but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain more about the person or the name’s contextual significance.

This verb means “cover with asphalt.” It describes the action of applying asphalt as a protective or sealing covering. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Genesis 6:14. Its meaning is specific and practical rather than a broad description of covering with any material. The surrounding verse supplies the particular object and purpose of the asphalt covering, while the word itself focuses on the act of coating or sealing.

This adjective describes something that comes too early, is not ready, or is unripe. It can refer to a time that is premature or to something that has not reached proper maturity. In the Greek Old Testament and related writings represented here, it occurs seven times, including passages in Job, Proverbs, Isaiah, and Wisdom. Its precise force depends on whether the surrounding passage concerns timing, maturity, or the condition of something not yet ready.

This verb means “dim-sighted,” describing someone whose eyesight is weak or impaired. It refers to limited visual ability rather than a figurative judgment or spiritual condition. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs once, in Genesis 48:10. Because the word appears only there and no verse text is provided here, its precise force in that sentence must be understood from the surrounding passage. Its basic meaning remains a description of impaired sight.

This adjective means “violent.” It describes a person, action, or event characterized by force, aggression, or harm, functioning as a describing word rather than naming an object or action by itself. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs 12 times across Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense appears in more than one setting. The surrounding verse determines what is being described, but the word itself points to violence or forceful behavior.

This word is a proper name, preserved in English-like form as “Galaaditidos” or “Galaathitithos,” rather than translated as an ordinary descriptive word. It identifies a named person, place, or group in the Greek Old Testament tradition, but the available wording does not specify which. It occurs nine times in the Greek LXX corpus, across both the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its exact reference depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This verb means “vigilant” or “watch,” describing someone who remains alert and attentive. It can refer to maintaining watch over a place, people, or circumstances rather than becoming careless or unaware. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs seven times, including three occurrences in Jeremiah. The wording may be rendered as watching, watched, or watch, but the central idea remains alert attention. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This noun means “dinner,” referring to a meal. It names the meal itself rather than an action, person, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs five times, including four occurrences in Daniel and one in 4 Maccabees. Its basic meaning remains simple: a dinner or meal mentioned in the surrounding account. The precise significance of any particular occurrence depends on the verse and its wider context.

gl: feed in a certain way; diet
d: feed in a certain way; diet

e.t: This verb means “feed in a certain way; diet.” It describes the manner or pattern by which someone is fed or takes nourishment, rather than simply naming food itself. As a verb, it expresses an action involving a person’s regular or directed nourishment. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus, it occurs once, at Job 30:7. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding context, but its basic meaning remains connected with feeding or following a diet.

This verb means “intend”: to have a purpose or plan to do something. It describes what someone has in mind or purposes, rather than merely an accidental action. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish Scriptures, it occurs 53 times, so it can describe human purposes across many kinds of passages. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This verb means to fill something up fully—to make it complete or full. It describes an action of bringing something to its full measure, rather than merely adding a small amount. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 4:40. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic idea is complete filling.

This adjective describes something that is hard to use or nearly useless. It can characterize a person, thing, or situation whose practical value is seriously limited, making it difficult to employ effectively. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings preserved in the LXX corpus, once in Isaiah and once in Wisdom. Its central idea is not merely inconvenience, but a condition in which usefulness is greatly reduced or almost absent.

Ezour, also known as Ezur, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. Its precise referent cannot be identified from the available lexical information alone. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 12:42. The name should therefore be understood as a specific designation, while the surrounding verse is needed to establish whom or what it identifies there.

This Greek LXX verb means “wipe off.” It describes removing something by wiping it away, rather than merely touching or moving it. The word appears three times in the LXX corpus, including passages in Sirach and the Epistle of Jeremiah. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on what is being wiped away and the surrounding verse, but its central idea is clear: cleansing or removing something from a surface through wiping.

gl: take oneself from a place; go abroad
d: take oneself from a place; go abroad

e.t: This verb means to take oneself away from a place or to go abroad. As a verb, it describes departure or relocation rather than an action performed on someone else. The wording focuses on the person leaving a location, so it can express withdrawal, departure, or travel to another country without specifying the reason. In the Greek LXX corpus, it appears once, at 2 Maccabees 8:13.

This Greek LXX noun means a “sore,” referring to an affected place on the body. It describes a physical condition that can appear on skin or flesh, rather than an action or quality. The word occurs 16 times in the Greek Old Testament, especially in passages concerning bodily afflictions and examination of the skin. Its ordinary sense remains simple and concrete: a sore or lesion on the body.

This Greek LXX verb means “block up”: to close or obstruct something so that passage or flow is stopped. It is used for actions such as stopping access, obstructing a route, or closing a water channel. The word occurs 20 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its central idea remains consistent across several settings: something is deliberately stopped or shut off. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being blocked.

This noun means “destruction”: the bringing of something to ruin or complete loss. It names a destructive outcome rather than the person or action causing it. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times, including passages in Psalms, Ezekiel, and 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains the collapse, removal, or ruin of what is destroyed.

This conjunction means “since in fact,” introducing a reason or basis for what has just been said or is about to be said. It connects one statement with another by presenting the second part as grounded in an actual circumstance. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it appears 20 times, including passages in Genesis, Exodus, Jeremiah, Daniel, and 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in a sentence depends on the surrounding words, but its central function is to mark a real reason or explanatory connection.

This Greek LXX verb means “double,” describing the action of making something twofold or causing it to have a doubled arrangement. It is an action word rather than a noun or name. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Exodus 26:9. The precise force of the action in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense is the doubling or making double of something. This word should be understood within the LXX corpus and not merged with a separate Greek New Testament entity.

This Greek LXX verb means “think on”—to turn something over in the mind or give it deliberate thought. It describes an act of mental consideration rather than merely noticing something. The word occurs four times in the Greek LXX corpus, in Job, Wisdom, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what the surrounding passage says is being considered. This word is distinct to the Greek LXX corpus and is not being identified here with a Greek New Testament word.

This Greek LXX adverb means “well,” describing something done, spoken, or experienced in a good, proper, or favorable way. It commonly modifies an action or statement, showing that it is done appropriately or turns out beneficially rather than merely identifying a person or thing. The word occurs 55 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented here, from Genesis through the Epistle of Jeremiah. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the action or statement it modifies.

This adverb describes doing something with reverence toward God or in a pious manner. It expresses the attitude or manner accompanying an action, rather than naming a person, object, or action itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 6:11. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central meaning is conduct marked by reverence and devotion.

This Greek LXX verb means “encourage” or “cheer.” It describes strengthening someone’s heart, giving courage, or lifting a person’s spirit. As a verb, it expresses an action done for another person rather than a quality someone merely possesses. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Esther 4:17. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse text and context, but its basic sense is to give someone courage and glad confidence.

Thenasa is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament text. It is rendered as “Thēnasa” or “Thinasa,” so the word identifies a named entity rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. Within the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 16:6. Its precise referent must be determined from that passage, since no broader definition or additional context is provided here.

This word is a proper name referring to a person named Iadia, also rendered Iathia. It functions as a personal designation rather than a description of an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, at 1 Chronicles 24:20 and Nehemiah 11:10. The name itself does not provide a broader definition or explain the person’s role; those details require the surrounding verse context.

Iarasia is a proper name, referring to a person named Iarasia rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name appears once, in 1 Chronicles 8:27. Because no surrounding verse text is available here, the name itself gives the person’s designation but does not establish further details about that individual. Its meaning is therefore best stated simply as the personal name “Iarasia.”

Iesia is a proper name, rendered as “Iesia.” It functions as a personal name rather than a general description, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs three times: once in 1 Chronicles, once in Ezra, and once in Nehemiah. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific identity or role in each passage cannot be stated further. The name itself remains the clearest meaning available here.

Iōazar, also rendered Ioazar, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies an individual in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 12:7. Because the available information gives the name and reference but not the verse text or surrounding passage, its precise role in that verse cannot be described further here. The name itself functions as a person’s designation.

This noun means “innovation” or “freshness,” expressing the quality of something new. It points to newness or originality rather than what is old, familiar, or unchanged. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in 1 Kings 8:53 and Ezekiel 47:12. These references establish its limited distribution in this corpus, while its central sense remains the idea of freshness or innovation. The precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

This verb means to squander or lavish something, describing the act of spending or using it freely and excessively. It presents resources as being poured out rather than carefully preserved. In the Greek LXX, it appears once, at Wisdom 5:13, so its exact force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The word itself centers on wasteful or extravagant use.

This verb means “cool down,” describing the action of becoming or making something less hot. It expresses a practical change in temperature rather than a person, object, or abstract quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Genesis 18:4. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding context, but its basic meaning remains the lowering or easing of heat. The word is therefore best understood as an action word connected with cooling.

This Greek LXX verb means to hold a useless opinion. It describes having or expressing a view that has no real value or benefit. The word focuses on the quality of the opinion rather than simply on the act of thinking or speaking. It occurs twice in the Greek text of 4 Maccabees, showing a specific verbal action rather than a general label for every kind of belief or judgment.

This noun means “renown”: the recognized fame or honor associated with a person. It describes how someone is known or esteemed publicly, rather than an action they perform. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both in Job—at Job 28:22 and Job 30:8. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This verb means “roll along” or “throw down.” It describes an action in which something is moved by rolling or cast downward. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Kings 9:33. Because it is an action word, its exact force depends on what is being moved and how the surrounding sentence presents that action; the basic idea remains rolling or throwing something down.

This Greek LXX verb means “prevent” or “withhold.” It describes stopping something from happening or holding something back so that it is not allowed to proceed or be given. As a verb, it normally expresses an action taken by someone to stop or hold back something. It appears 27 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books represented by this LXX corpus.

Ladan is a personal name, also rendered Lathan. It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name appears three times, all within 1 Chronicles 26:21. The available record gives the name itself but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain Ladan’s family role or significance in that passage. Its meaning here is therefore the personal designation “Ladan; Lathan.”

This verb means “stone”: to attack or kill someone by throwing stones. It describes an action rather than a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 27 times, all in Old Testament verses, showing that it is used repeatedly for this kind of physical punishment or attack. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This noun refers to a destroyer or spoiler—a person who causes ruin, damage, or loss. It describes someone characterized by destructive action rather than merely naming destruction itself. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, the word occurs twice, both occurrences being in 4 Maccabees 18:8. The precise force of the word in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning remains one who damages or destroys what might otherwise remain sound.

This word refers to an “inclosed space”—a place bounded or enclosed rather than open and unrestricted. It is used as a noun or adjective, so it can identify such a contained place or describe something associated with one. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 11 times across 11 verses, including passages in Samuel, Chronicles, Psalms, and Song of Songs. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains an enclosed space.

Marmēna, also rendered Marmina, is a personal name rather than a general term describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 2:49. The available information identifies the name itself but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain the person’s role or significance. Its meaning is therefore best understood simply as the proper name of an individual mentioned in that genealogy or historical record.

Νεῦμα means “nod”: a movement of the head or a nodding gesture used to communicate without spoken words. As a noun in the LXX corpus, it names the gesture itself rather than an action such as speaking or commanding. It occurs twice in this corpus, once in Isaiah and once in 2 Maccabees. The surrounding verse text is needed to determine what the nod communicates in either passage.

This noun means “grazing” or “spreading.” It can refer to the activity of animals feeding in pasture, or to something extending outward or becoming widespread. The precise sense depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is movement or provision extending across an area. In the Greek Old Testament, including its deuterocanonical books, it occurs 31 times, showing that it is used in more than one setting while retaining these basic meanings.

This adjective means “short-lived,” describing something whose life or duration is brief rather than long. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in Job. The word focuses on limited length of life or existence, not on a particular emotion, moral quality, or event. Its exact force in a verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains brevity of life.

This noun means “small bird,” referring to a little bird rather than a particular species named by the word itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 13 times, all in Leviticus 14, where the text repeatedly speaks of birds used in the cleansing procedure for a person or house. The word’s basic sense remains simple: a small bird considered in the instructions. Its precise significance in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Ouaphrē, also rendered Uafri, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular person or place by name within the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Jeremiah 51:30. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific identity and role cannot be explained further, but its basic function is clear: it serves as a personal name in that passage.

Pathaia, also written Pathea, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies an individual and appears once, in Nehemiah 11:24. The available information preserves the name itself but does not provide a meaning beyond these name forms. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person being identified there.

gl: loosening by the side: paralysis; palsy
d: loosening by the side: paralysis; palsy

e.t: This noun refers to paralysis or palsy—a condition understood as a loosening or loss of strength in part of the body. Its central sense is physical inability or weakness, rather than an action or command. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Ezekiel 21:15. The precise force of the word there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which are needed to explain its use in context.

This verb means “exasperate”: to provoke someone until they become deeply irritated or frustrated. It describes an action that strains patience and can lead a person toward anger or discouragement. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 42 times, so it is a recurring way of describing conduct that aggravates or provokes others. Its exact force in any verse depends on who is being provoked and the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “encampment” or “barracks”: a place where people are gathered and lodged as a camp. It can refer to an organized camp rather than merely the act of camping. The word occurs 284 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, showing that it is a regularly used term for a camp or barracks setting. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

gl: invite sb to eat a memorial dinner
d: invite sb to eat a memorial dinner

e.t: This verb means to invite someone to eat a memorial dinner. It describes the act of arranging or extending such an invitation, rather than simply the act of eating. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Samuel 3:35. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning centers on inviting another person to share a meal held in memory of someone.

“Pine” is a noun referring to a pine tree. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, once in Ezekiel and once in Zechariah, with singular and plural English renderings reflecting the number of trees mentioned. The word identifies a kind of tree rather than an action, quality, or person. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here.

This Greek LXX verb means “bring near”—to cause someone or something to come closer. It describes an action of drawing near rather than merely being nearby. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 6:4. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and scene, but its basic meaning remains the movement or bringing of someone or something into closer proximity.

e.h: A Word for For A Long Time
e.t: This word is an adjective that describes a quality or condition. Its basic sense is “for a long time”. It describes something extended over a considerable period rather than brief or immediate. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears six times across six verses, including passages in Genesis, Job, Wisdom, 4 Maccabees, and the Epistle of Jeremiah. The surrounding verse determines exactly what receives this description, but the central idea remains duration: something lasting or continuing for a long time.

This Greek LXX word describes something lying face downward or appearing swollen and distended. It can function as an adjective describing a person or thing, and it may also be used as a noun for one characterized in that way. The word occurs four times in the Greek deuterocanonical writings, including Wisdom and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains a prone position or a distended condition.

This adjective means “at hand; ready,” describing something available, prepared, or within reach. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 11:3. Its basic sense points to readiness or immediate availability rather than a specific object or action. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what is described there, but the word itself presents something as close at hand or prepared for use. This is a Greek LXX word and should be understood within that translation’s wording and context.

This Greek LXX noun means “sprinkling,” referring to the act of sprinkling rather than to a person or object. It occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament, all within Numbers 19, where the word is used in connection with the instructions recorded in that chapter. Its basic sense is therefore the application or scattering of a substance by sprinkling. The precise force in each occurrence depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

Rasōn, also rendered Rhason, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person or named figure in the Greek Septuagint text. This name occurs twice in the LXX corpus, once in Ezra 2:48 and once in Nehemiah 7:50. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context, which is not included here.

Raphou, also written Rhafu, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Numbers 13:9, so its normal lexical function is simply to identify a person or named figure. The available information does not provide a broader definition or explain the name’s etymology. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person being identified there.

This noun means a broadsword, a large, powerful sword used as a weapon. It names a physical weapon rather than an abstract idea, and its normal sense remains consistent across the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings. The word occurs 227 times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing especially often in prophetic, historical, and poetic books. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the basic meaning is a broad sword or substantial weapon.

Saria is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 9:44. Because it is a personal name, its meaning here is chiefly identification: it distinguishes the individual called Saria. The name itself does not provide enough information to explain that person’s character, role, or significance without the surrounding verse and passage.

Saron is a proper name, used as a personal or place name rather than as a descriptive word with a general meaning. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times, in Joshua, 1 Chronicles, and Isaiah. Its English rendering remains “Saron,” reflecting that the word identifies Saron rather than translating an ordinary quality or action. The exact person or place intended in any particular verse must be understood from that verse’s surrounding context.

Sikima is a proper name rendered as “Sikima.” It functions as a distinctive name rather than a general description or action word. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs nine times across seven verses, including passages in Genesis, 1 Kings, Psalms, and Hosea. The name itself identifies what is being referred to, while the surrounding verse determines its specific significance in each occurrence.

Souri, also rendered Suri, is a proper name used to identify a person in the Greek Old Testament. Because it is a name rather than a descriptive word, it does not itself express an action, quality, or spiritual idea; the surrounding verse identifies whom it names. In this LXX corpus, it occurs twice, once in Numbers 13:5 and once in 1 Chronicles 25:3. Those references show its use as a personal designation, while the name alone does not provide further information about the person.

This noun means “little sparrow,” referring to a small bird. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs ten times across ten verses. Its meaning is simple and concrete: it identifies a sparrow, with emphasis on its smallness. The surrounding verse determines how the bird is being mentioned, but the word itself names the bird rather than an action, quality, or abstract idea.

This adjective means “planted together,” describing things joined or growing together rather than existing separately. It presents a picture of shared rooting, close attachment, or combined growth.
